title: Music & Sound
strapline: Bang it, shake it, sing it again — rhythm in their bodies and songs by heart.
intent: Move from making sounds to controlling them: loud and quiet, fast and slow, start and — hardest of all — stop
Feel steady beat and rhythm patterns in the body — the groundwork that later phonics stands on
Grow a real repertoire of songs known by heart, asked for by name and sung without an adult
Sharpen listening: matching sounds, guessing hidden ones, hearing the syllables inside names and words
Experience the togetherness of group music — everyone stopping at once is a social achievement
Pick up the language of music: louder, softer, faster, slower, high, low
implementation: Keep instruments accessible every day — a cupboard opened on Fridays teaches children that music is rationed
Sing through the day: tidy-up songs, name songs at group time, and take requests — children asking for a song by name is the goal
Play stop-and-start and loud-and-quiet games with a conductor — and hand the conducting to a child as soon as you can
Clap the syllables in names and favourite words playfully: "O-li-ver — three claps!"
Copy a child's rhythm back to them before offering a new one — serve and return, in sound
Teach songs slowly and repeat them often; a deep repertoire beats constant novelty
Make sound-makers together — shakers with different fillings — then listen, compare and guess
key_questions: Can you make it whisper? Now can you make it thunder?
Whose name has the most claps?
What do you think is inside this shaker? How can you tell?
Which song shall we sing — how do you ask for that one?
Can you copy my pattern — tap, tap, shake?

impact.text: Our youngest musicians bang, shake and tap on purpose and delight in the effect — cause and effect you can hear.
Children join in songs with the actions and ask for favourites by name, again and again.
Familiar songs surface in play — sung from memory, sometimes quietly to a doll or to nobody at all.
Children clap along to the syllables in songs and names, and throw themselves into rhyming games.
Rhythm becomes pattern: children copy tap-tap-shake, keep it going, invent their own, and can say what comes next.
Children learn new songs quickly and experiment freely — faster, slower, whispered, roared, and gloriously silly versions.
Ears sharpen: children hear rhyme, initial sounds and syllables in playful games — phonics readiness built through play, not worksheets.
Older children own a wide repertoire — fifteen-plus songs by heart — and sing, move and perform with confidence, feeding that language back into their play.

enhancements: A conductor's spot and baton — the child in charge decides loud, quiet, go and STOP
Homemade shakers with secret fillings (rice, buttons, sand) for a listen-and-guess game
An outdoor sound wall: pans, pipes, bottles and beaters on the fence
A song basket of props — a spider, a star, a bus — so children can request by object before they can request by name
Sound walks around the local streets: what can we hear, and who's making it?
A simple recorder app moment: capture the band, play it back, watch the faces
Songs and rhymes from our families' home languages, taught to everyone

playing_exploring: Instruments reward pure exploration — every surface, shake and scrape makes something new to hear
Children bring music into their own play uninvited, which is exactly the point
active_learning: Keeping a beat, waiting for the stop and mastering a tricky rhyme all take happy, repeated effort
creating_thinking: Children invent their own verses, rhythms and silly versions — changing a known song is creativity working on memory
Predicting what comes next in a rhythm or rhyme is early pattern-thinking they can feel
